🚨🇲🇽 <u>Navy Captures CJNG-Linked Regional Boss in Southern Veracruz</u>

Mexico's Navy (Semar) arrested Samuel de la Cruz Anaya, alias "Panda," in Coatzacoalcos, Veracruz. The Security Cabinet identifies him as the regional leader of a CJNG-linked group operating in Jáltipan, Cosoleacaque and Minatitlán, dedicated to kidnapping, extortion, drug dealing and fuel theft.

The case began in January 2026 with the kidnapping of two businessmen in Cosoleacaque. That same month, a safe house in Jáltipan was dismantled and a lieutenant, alias "Sparta," was detained. Ten months of naval intelligence later, the boss himself fell. He carried an arrest warrant for kidnapping; 398,000 pesos in cash were seized.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>Tamaulipas Governor Demands the INE and State Electoral Body Open Their Contracts</u>

Governor Américo Villarreal called on the INE and the Tamaulipas Electoral Institute (IETAM) to investigate the network of electoral-material suppliers. He wants contracts, amounts, suppliers and award procedures made public, and any links between the companies and electoral officials reviewed.

"As our President has said, this business structure did not arise or begin in this administration or the previous one," Villarreal said. He noted that Guadalupe Taddei was appointed head of Sonora's electoral body in 2014, under Lorenzo Córdova's INE, and reached the INE presidency in 2023 by lottery in the Chamber of Deputies, not by Morena's choice.

🚨🇲🇽 <u>Supreme Court Strikes Down Puebla's Electoral Reform, Restores Minority Seats</u>

Mexico's Supreme Court invalidated the Puebla Congress's July 28 reform that gave 11 of the capital's 15 city council seats to the winning party and left four for everyone else. The PAN had challenged it.

The Court ordered the next municipal election to use a 10-5 split: ten seats for the winner, five by proportional representation. The reporting justice argued that proportional representation must guarantee real minority participation, and that restricting it weakens democratic debate. Justices Lenia Batres, Irving Espinosa Betanzo and María Estela Ríos dissented, saying the ruling invaded the legislature's powers.

This is the Court the opposition swore would be a rubber stamp. It just ruled for the PAN against a Morena-led state congress.

🇲🇽💰 <u>Mexico's 2027 Budget Clears Committee: 10.6 Trillion Pesos, a Trillion for Social Programs</u>

The Chamber of Deputies' Budget Committee approved Sheinbaum's 2027 spending plan in general, 33 votes to 12. Morena and its allies voted yes, and so did Movimiento Ciudadano; only PAN and PRI voted no.

Total spending: 10 trillion 636 billion pesos, a 1.3% real increase over 2026. Priority social programs get just over 1 trillion pesos, 2.6% of GDP. Investment spending reaches 1.13 trillion, 90.5% of it in physical infrastructure. The INE's request was cut by 5 billion pesos.

The full chamber debates and votes next week, Monday through Wednesday.

🇲🇽🌎 <u>Tequila Takes On India's 150% Tariff</u>

Mexican tequila exports to India grew more than 30% between 2024 and 2025, to about 2 million liters a year, despite a 150% tariff. Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard says the terms of reference are set, India's trade minister has committed to cutting it, and the deal gets signed in 2027: "If you don't want to lower the tariff on tequila, you don't want anything to do with me, because tequila is a symbol." The US still takes 82% of tequila exports. (El Financiero)

🇲🇽🎨 <u>Zócalo's Giant Catrina: 1.6 Million Visitors in Four Days</u>

Mexico City's Monumental Catrina, more than 33 meters tall and recognized by Guinness, drew 1.6 million visitors to the Zócalo in four days. Tourism, food and Day of the Dead festivities brought in more than 15 billion pesos. Add Formula 1, and the city's total reached 36 billion. By popular demand, she stays until November 11.

🇲🇽🌎 <u>Mexico Heads to COP31: "Mexico Is Back"</u>

Mexico arrives at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey (November 9–20) with ground to make up: in 2025 it generated a quarter of its electricity from low-carbon sources, only 13% from renewables, and 74% from fossil fuels. The 2025–2030 plan to strengthen and expand the national grid would add 22,000 MW. "One of the important messages to the COP is that Mexico is back," Adrián Fernández of the Iniciativa Climática de México told IPS.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>The INE's Favorite Suppliers Came From the CISEN</u>

José Alfredo and Raymundo Hernández Casillas, the brothers behind the ballot-supply network now under investigation, started at Gobernación in 1983 and moved to the CISEN, the PRI-era political intelligence agency, in 1989 under Salinas. Anti-Corruption Secretary Raquel Buenrostro laid out the trail: their front companies won more than 2 billion pesos in contracts from 23 of the 32 state electoral bodies between 2014 and 2023, without owning the machinery to make electoral materials. Their old boss at the CISEN, Juan Carlos Padilla Aguilar, now sits in the leadership of the right-wing party Somos, the same party as Lorenzo Córdova.

🇲🇽🏭 <u>Topolobampo: Ammonia Plant Machinery Heads Back to the US</u>

Heavy equipment for Proman-GPO's planned ammonia plant at Topolobampo, Sinaloa, is being pulled out. Supplier Fagioli's temporary import permits are expiring, and the machinery has to be back in the US by November 15. The company insists the project isn't cancelled. The Mayo-Yoreme "¡Aquí No!" collective, camped outside for more than 150 days, calls it a win and vows to keep fighting for Ohuira Bay, a Ramsar-listed wetland.

🇲🇽💧 <u>Mexico's "Water Millionaires": 1.1% of Users Hold 22.3% of the Water</u>

An Ibero study of Mexico's public water-rights registry (REPDA) found that 3,304 users (966 companies, 1,537 individuals and 800 civil associations) hold 22.3% of all water concessioned in the country. That's 1.1% of all users. In 2020, 115 of Mexico's 653 aquifers were overexploited, and the "water millionaires" were drawing from 99 of them. This is the map that Salinas' 1992 National Water Law drew when it turned water into concessions.
